newsitem.title: CANADA: FORECAST-Canadian yield curve seen flattening.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST-Canadian yield curve seen flattening.

text.p: The Canadian yield curve is expected to flatten sharply during the next two years amid central bank tightening and a gradual decline in long bond yields, a Reuters poll of economists showed on Wednesday.
The quarterly survey polled 27 economists in Canada and the United States on their forecasts for Canadian interest rates and bond yields going out to the fourth quarter of 1999.
The flattening of the yield curve was among the major trends uncovered by the survey.

The survey showed the yield curve, as measured by the difference between the 30-year benchmark bond and three-month cash T-bill, was expected to narrow by more than 100 basis points in the next two years.

The gap in yields between the 30-year bond and three-month T-bill was 404 basis points on Wednesday. Economists expected that to narrow to 328 basis points by the first quarter of 1998 and 289 basis points by the first quarter of 1999.

While the expected flattening may appear dramatic, analysts said it was consistent with the outlook for the Canadian economy. Canada's growth rate is expected to surpass three percent in each quarter of 1997, likely prompting the Bank of Canada to start raising rates after 11 rate cuts in 1996.

Canada's central bank has kept monetary conditions easy in Canada because economic growth has remained well below potential. But with the pickup in growth and the narrowing of the output gap, the Bank was widely expected to change its stance.

"(Curve flattening) is completely consistent with the idea of the output gap closing as (Bank of Canada Governor Gordon) Thiessen mentioned in his speech last week. As that excess slack is lessened, we'll have less accommodative monetary conditions," said Mark Chandler, a senior economist with Goldman Sachs Canada.

Even as short-term Canadian interest rates rise in the coming quarters, analysts surveyed in the Reuters poll expect long bond yields eventually to decline from current levels. Canada's 30-year benchmark bond traded with a yield of 7.164 percent on Wednesday.

The survey results showed 30-year bond yields expected to trade above current levels for the rest of 1997, mirroring gains in economic growth. But as Canada's economic growth rate falls below 3.0 percent in the first quarter of 1998, bond yields are seen falling below current levels and declining further during the remainder of 1998.
Analysts said the decline in yields beginning in 1998 would be largely a function of the effect on the Canadian and U.S. economies of central bank tightening.

"I would say by late in this year and into early next year as economic performance starts to stumble (long bond) yields will start to fall," said Jeoff Hall, Canadian analyst with Technical Data. "We're going to move flatter in Canada and it's going to be a function of the slowdown in the respective economies."
Chandler said the expected drop in yields in 1998 was conditional on whether the rate hikes in the United States and Canada were effective in slowing economic growth and dampening inflation.
